finding.claim: GET /users has no authentication or authorization. The org filter comes straight from the query string, so any caller can list id and name for every user in any organization (IDOR / broken access control). The SQL itself is parameterized, so this is not SQL injection.
finding.source: req.query.org on an unauthenticated GET /users request
finding.sink: req.pg.query("SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE org = $1") returning rows via res.json

trace.note: Route registered with no auth middleware. No app.use() exists anywhere in the file.
req.query.org is used directly as the tenant filter. It is not compared with any session or user org.
All matching rows are returned to the caller.

finding.guards_checked: Checked for app.use auth or session middleware, a comparison of the caller's org with the requested org, and a role check. None exist in db.js. This is the only file in the directory, so auth middleware that sets req.pg could exist elsewhere, but nothing here ties the query to a caller identity. The query is parameterized ($1), which rules out injection. Also checked: /file is guarded by path.resolve plus a startsWith(ROOT + path.sep) check, so traversal is blocked. /count uses execFile with fixed arguments, so there is no command injection.

verdict.guard_found: none (only parameterized $1 query at db.js:9, which prevents SQLi but not access control; no auth middleware or org comparison in db.js)
verdict.reason: db.js:8-10 registers GET /users with no auth middleware and passes attacker-controlled req.query.org as the tenant filter, returning all matching rows, so an anonymous caller can enumerate any org's users (req.pg is set elsewhere, but nothing in the available code ties the query to a caller identity).
